newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Pope in Prague warns against Western hedonism.
newsitem.headline: Pope in Prague warns against Western hedonism.

text.p: Pope John Paul holds a mass with young people on Saturday to mark the 1,000th anniversary of a saint's death after starting a visit to the Czech Republic with a stern warning against hedonism imported from the West.

The 76-year-old Pontiff travels to the town of Hradec Kralove, some 100 km (60 miles) east of Prague to commemorate St Adalbert, the first bishop of Czech origin who took the gospel to Poland and is seen by Catholics as a symbol of European Christian unity.

But the Pope, on his third trip to Prague since the fall of communism, said on Friday that Czechs faced a "grave social malaise" as they built a free market economy after more than 40 years of communism.

In a speech to Czech bishops in the Vatican's Prague embassy the Pope criticised "hedonism, which has invaded these lands from neighbouring countries, and contributed to a growing crisis of values in everyday life".

He said Czech society faced danger from "the infiltration of certain ideas already widespread in the West". He denounced the Czechs' high abortion rate and said the spread of pornography, prostitution and paedophilia were "symptomatic of a situation of grave social malaise".
The Polish Pope, who influenced events that led to the collapse of communism in Europe, has frequently warned Eastern Europeans against excessive materialism.
The Czech Republic has one of the highest standards of living of the former East bloc. But it is also a highly secularised society and few people attend church.
The Pontiff said Czech society was still paying a high price for 40 years of repression of the church under communism.
But he paid warm tribute to Czech President Vaclav Havel, a former dissident playwright imprisoned by the communists, saying he was "among those who brought about the rebirth of this country".

In an earlier written address to the Pontifical Academy of Social Sciences, before he left for Prague, Pope John Paul told an audience of academics and bankers that people were more important than profit.
"Unfortunately, experience illustrates that a market economy, left to unconditional freedom, is far from bringing the greatest possible advantage to people and societies," he said.
Havel, who greeted the Pope at Prague airport, said Czech civilisation faced subtle threats.
"Like everyone else, we too have to deal with them, and have so far proved rather inept at that," he said.
Havel, seen by many as the nation's leading moral authority, has also frequently cautioned against importing "Western junk culture", calling instead for spiritual renewal.

In a speech at the airport, he said Adalbert, or Vojtech in Czech, saw his homeland as part of the European Christian community. "This community was to be based on a spiritual and moral renewal and on readiness to embrace common values -- which is needed today just as it was then.
The Pope, whose health has been fragile in recent years, walked slowly but unaided and stood as he delivered a speech at the airport.
He is also due to hold an open-air mass in Prague on Sunday then meet other church leaders in ecumenical worship in the city's St Vitus Cathedral before leaving for Rome.
